strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formulated problem: knowledge distillation under unknown covariate shift where spurious features appear during training but not at test time. The paper correctly identifies an important gap in the KD literature.

The proposed ConfG method is conceptually elegant: it leverages teacher-student disagreement to guide a diffusion model to synthesize challenging samples that target the student's spurious shortcuts, without requiring explicit knowledge of what those spurious features are. This is a meaningful advance over prior diffusion-based augmentation methods (GIF, DistDiff, DAFusion, ActGen).

Strong and consistent empirical results: ConfG substantially improves worst-group accuracy on CelebA (from 54.0% to 66.1% over the best baseline in the full EDRM+CutMix setting) and SpuCo Birds (52.7% to 62.7%), and improves spurious mAUC on Spurious ImageNet. The improvements are consistent across multiple evaluation metrics.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation and ablations, including the number of synthetic augmentations, combination with standard augmentation techniques (MixUp, AutoAugment, CutMixPick), different student architectures (ViT-T, TinyViT, ResNet-18), larger training datasets, and cost-vs-quality trade-offs (5x and 10x expansions of baselines still underperform ConfG's 2x).

The inclusion of a theoretical investigation (Proposition 1 and Lemma 1 in Appendix A.1) provides useful motivation for why the confidence-guided augmentation reduces the generalization gap |Omega|, even if the assumptions are strong.

Good qualitative analysis (Figures 3, 4, 6, 7, 8) showing that ConfG successfully removes spurious features while preserving causal ones, and interestingly it also revealed an unintended spurious correlation (blue eyes) not part of the dataset attributes.
Honest and clear discussion of limitations (teacher availability and computational cost), and appropriate acknowledgment of when the method would and would not apply.
weaknesses: The primary limitation, acknowledged by the authors, is that the method requires a teacher that is robust to the covariate shift. On SpuCo Birds, the CLIP teacher was insufficient and they had to fine-tune a ViT-B on the full balanced dataset, which would not be possible in practice. This substantially limits the practical applicability of the method, and the paper would be strengthened by more analysis of how teacher robustness affects downstream performance.

The experimental setting is somewhat artificial: the covariate shift is created by deliberately removing entire groups from the training set, and the spurious features are known to the authors. It is unclear how ConfG behaves in more realistic settings where the shift is more gradual or where no balanced validation data exists to calibrate the teacher.

The theoretical analysis (Proposition 1) relies on strong assumptions (e.g., the student approximates the teacher well on the training support, the teacher approximates p* within delta_t on both train and test supports, and delta_t + delta_s < 1/L). These assumptions may not hold under realistic covariate shift, and the condition Theta > 0 is difficult to verify in practice. The connection between the theory and the practical method is therefore somewhat loose.

The computational cost is non-trivial: ConfG requires 11.4 sec/image (5 optimization steps with decode) versus 2.1 sec for standard SD and 3.3 sec for ActGen. While the paper argues that fewer high-quality augmentations outperform more low-quality ones, this overhead may still be a barrier for larger-scale applications, and there is no analysis of how cost scales with the number of classes or image resolution.

Some experimental details raise minor questions: the final student is distilled on a joint dataset of real images and synthetic augmentations, but the paper does not fully ablate whether the student model used for generation (the 'auxiliary' student) could be replaced with a cheaper heuristic; also, the effect of the nonlinearity gamma=2 is only empirically justified.

The novelty relative to ActGen is incremental: ActGen also uses the downstream student's loss to guide generation; ConfG's main difference is the teacher-student disagreement objective and the null-text-inversion-based latent optimization. The paper does not compare computational cost fairly when comparing to baselines that use more augmentations.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: knowledge distillation under unknown covariate shift, where spurious features are present at training but absent at test time. The framing of 'can a student become robust to spurious features it cannot observe, given only a robust teacher?' is crisp and interesting.

The method (ConfiG) is conceptually elegant and novel. Rather than requiring explicit knowledge of spurious features or group labels, it uses the teacher-student disagreement as a signal to guide a diffusion model to synthesize hard samples that target the student's reliance on spurious shortcuts. This is a clean idea that directly operationalizes the insight that teacher/student agreement is low on underrepresented groups.

Strong and consistent empirical results. Table 1 and Table 12/13 show ConfiG outperforming strong diffusion-based baselines (DAFusion, DistDiff, GIF, ActGen) on CelebA and SpuCo Birds across group mean, worst group, and sample mean accuracy, with meaningful margins (e.g., worst-group 66.1% vs 54.0% on CelebA). Improvements on Spurious ImageNet mAUCC further support generality beyond group-shift settings.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix A.1 (Proposition 1 and Lemma 1) provides a principled justification that confidence-guided augmentations provably reduce |Ω| under stated assumptions, giving the method a solid foundation rather than a purely heuristic construction.

Comprehensive ablation suite: number of synthetic augmentations (Fig. 5), different student architectures (TinyViT, ResNet-18), larger training set (Table 7), quality-vs-quantity (Table 8), combination with TAB (Tables 3, 11), and ERM+EDRM combination (Table 9). These substantially strengthen the empirical case.

The 'quality over quantity' result (Table 8) is a valuable finding: baselines with 5x/10x augmentations still underperform ConfiG with 2x, and are comparable in compute, which directly addresses the natural concern about the higher per-image generation cost.

Good qualitative evidence (Figures 4, 6, 7, 8) that ConfiG changes spurious attributes while preserving causal ones, plus the interesting observation that ConfiG surfaced an unlabeled spurious correlation (blond hair / blue eyes) it was not explicitly told about, supporting the 'unknown spurious features' claim.
Reproducibility is well-supported: hyperparameter tables, prompts for null-text inversion, optimizer details, and clear descriptions of baselines and training setup are provided.
The paper is clearly written and well organized, with an effective motivating figure (Figure 1) and a transparent limitations section.
weaknesses: The central assumption of a robust teacher is strong and, by the authors' own admission, not always satisfiable in practice. On SpuCo Birds the CLIP teacher's worst-group accuracy was only 40.2%, forcing the authors to fine-tune a ViT-B on the full balanced training set to obtain a usable teacher — a procedure explicitly noted as not possible in practice. This means the method's applicability hinges on teacher robustness that may not exist for genuinely unknown spurious features, which somewhat tempers the 'unknown covariate shift' claim.

Computational overhead is non-trivial: ConfiG requires decoding at every optimization step (11.4 sec/image vs 2.1 sec for vanilla SD and 3.3 sec for ActGen). Although the paper argues this is offset by quality (Table 8), the practical cost and reliance on a latent diffusion model plus null-text inversion is a real barrier for scaling to large datasets.

The theoretical guarantee (Proposition 1) relies on several strong assumptions: the teacher approximates p* within δt on the support of both train and test distributions, the student approximates the teacher within δs on the training support, and δt + δs < 1/L. While the paper discusses their realism, these are fairly restrictive conditions, and the bound's practical tightness is not empirically validated.

The method requires an auxiliary student trained on real images only to serve as the disagreement source, adding an extra training stage and a degree of sensitivity to that auxiliary student's quality that is not fully analyzed.
The choice γ = 2 in Eq. 7 is stated to be empirical ('we find γ = 2 to perform well'), but no sensitivity analysis over γ is provided, leaving the robustness of this design choice unclear.

The evaluation of covariate shift focuses on complete absence of groups or class-level spurious features with a binary spurious attribute. It is not clear how the approach would extend to continuous, multi-attribute, or partially overlapping spurious correlations, which limits the generality of the empirical claims.

The student's worst-group accuracy is ultimately bounded by the teacher's (66.7% on CelebA, 95.1% on SpuCo Birds), so the achievable gains depend heavily on the teacher ceiling; the paper could more explicitly characterize when ConfiG helps versus when the teacher itself is the bottleneck.

strengths: Well-motivated problem framing: the paper clearly identifies that a distilled student under covariate shift learns spurious shortcuts, and demonstrates this with the teacher-student agreement plot (Fig. 2) showing large disagreement on groups absent from training data.

Simple and intuitive method: maximizing teacher-student disagreement via guided latent diffusion is a clean idea that naturally targets spurious features without requiring explicit knowledge of them, and the nonlinear transform for amplifying gradients is a sensible engineering detail.

Empirical results on CelebA and SpuCo Birds are consistent and sometimes substantial: ConfiG outperforms four diffusion-based augmentation baselines across group-mean and worst-group accuracy, e.g. +12 worst-group over ActGen under CutMix+EDRM, and matches the teacher's worst-group accuracy on CelebA.

Thorough ablation suite: number of synthetic augmentations, alternative student architectures (TinyViT, ResNet-18), larger training sets, cost-vs-quality tradeoff, combination with TAB, and ERM+EDRM mixing are all investigated, lending credibility to the claims.
Honest limitations section acknowledging the teacher dependency, plus qualitative examples (Figs. 3, 4, 6-8) that support the claimed mechanism of altering spurious while retaining causal features.
weaknesses: The method fundamentally requires a robust teacher, and this dependency undercuts the "unknown covariate shift" premise. On SpuCo Birds the CLIP teacher has only 40.2% worst-group accuracy, so the authors fine-tune a ViT-B on the balanced SpuCo dataset that contains the groups absent from the student's training data. The teacher therefore has effectively seen the shifted distribution, and the student's robustness is largely inherited from it; the setup is closer to "robust teacher transfers robustness" than to solving an unknown shift.

The theoretical contribution (Proposition 1) rests on restrictive assumptions (bounded teacher and student approximation errors with δ_t + δ_s < 1/L, augmentation support exactly equal to the disagreement set defined by t_y(x) ≥ τ, f_y(x) ≤ σ). The proof is a fairly direct cross-entropy bounding argument and largely restates the design intuition rather than providing new insight; it does not cover the failure modes observed in practice (e.g., weak teachers).

Gains on Spurious ImageNet are marginal and somewhat inconsistently reported: ConfiG improves over ActGen by only 0.1 val acc / 0.3 mAUC on ViT-T, yet the text claims it "surpasses all baselines by at least 0.5% mAUC," which does not match the ViT-T numbers. This weakens the generalization claim to class-wise spurious features.

Novelty over ActGen is incremental. Both use an auxiliary student for augmentation; the main change is swapping ActGen's student-CE objective for a teacher-student disagreement objective. Disagreement-based sample selection is well established in active learning, and the paper does not position this connection or show the objective change is the key factor in a controlled way.

All experiments are on very small, artificially constructed subsets (500 training images, 250/class; larger-set ablation only 750/class) with deliberately removed groups, so it is unclear whether the conclusions hold at realistic scales or under more natural, less perfectly correlated shifts.

Computational cost is substantial: 11.4 s/image versus 3.3 s for ActGen (≈3.5x) due to per-step decoding during guided optimization. While the authors argue quality beats quantity, this is a real practical drawback that is only partially mitigated.

It is not fully disentangled whether the very low student accuracy (37.2%) and high loss (R=3.00) on ConfiG augmentations reflect genuinely informative hard samples or simply out-of-distribution/degraded generations; some qualitative examples (Figs. 6-7) do look distorted, and the paper does not provide a quantitative check that class semantics are preserved in the augmentations.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: knowledge distillation under unknown covariate shift, where limited training-data coverage causes students to rely on spurious features and fail on unseen groups. The proposed ConfiG method is well motivated and novel in its use of teacher-student disagreement to guide diffusion-based data augmentation.

The empirical evaluation is comprehensive: four datasets (CelebA-HQ, SpuCo Birds, BAR, ImageNet-100), six diffusion-based augmentation baselines, group-aware metrics (SMA/GMA/WGA) plus spurious score, and compute-matched comparisons. ConfiG achieves best or second-best results across most settings and delivers large worst-group accuracy gains.

The paper includes extensive ablations and analyses, including individual components (inter-class mixing vs. latent optimization), stronger standard augmentations, scaling the number of augmentations, weaker teachers, different student/teacher architectures, model-centric bias mitigation, replacement probability, and compute/FLOP costs. This strengthens the empirical case.
The theoretical section and appendix provide additional motivation, implementation details, hyperparameters, failure cases, and qualitative examples, supporting reproducibility and transparency.

The authors explicitly discuss limitations, including the focus on classification and global augmentations, dependence on pre-trained teacher models, and the fact that augmentation affects both Ω and Ψ. These are appropriate and do not invalidate the main contribution.
weaknesses: The theoretical result offers limited practical guidance: it relies on strong assumptions and constants (e.g., Q, Θ, α, κ_t, Δ_p) that are not estimable in practice, and it does not fully account for the fact that augmented training data also influences Ψ, not only Ω. The proposition is useful as motivation but is weaker than the empirical claims suggest.

The synthetic augmentations may be adversarial or artifacted, and the paper does not provide a quantitative realism/diversity evaluation or human study. It is possible that some gains come from exploiting classifier errors rather than genuinely removing spurious features, although the DiG-IN regularization, failure-case analysis, and qualitative examples partially mitigate this concern.

Hyperparameter sensitivity is incomplete: γ is fixed to 2 without sensitivity analysis, and prompt templates, inversion steps, and target-class selection require design choices. ImageNet-100 results appear to be single-run without standard deviations, making the statistical evidence less strong than for the group-shift datasets.

Evaluation is confined to controlled benchmarks where biases are artificially induced by subsampling known groups or places. Performance under natural, fully unknown covariate shifts and real-world data collection conditions remains unverified, despite the paper's framing around unknown covariate shift.

The per-augmentation computational and engineering cost remains high: ConfiG requires multiple optimization steps and an auxiliary student model, and although FLOPs are matched by generating fewer augmentations than baselines, wall-clock cost, memory overhead, and scalability to larger foundation-model teachers are not fully characterized.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and challenging problem: knowledge distillation under unknown covariate shift and group robustness without group annotations.
The empirical motivation is clear: teacher-student disagreement concentrates on groups absent from training data (Fig. 2, Table 1), which justifies targeting such regions.

ConfiG is technically sound and clearly described: differentiable latent optimization of a diffusion model guided by teacher-student confidence, warm-started by inter-class mixing and prompt-to-prompt editing.

Experiments are extensive and convincing across CelebA-HQ, SpuCo Birds, BAR, and ImageNet-100, with strong improvements in worst-group and mean-group accuracy over several diffusion augmentation baselines.

The ablation studies are thorough, covering individual components, stronger standard augmentations, scaling augmentations per image, weaker teachers, single-step diffusion, different architectures, replacement probabilities, target class choice, and model-centric bias mitigation.
The theoretical proposition, while assumption-heavy, provides useful intuition about why challenging augmentations can reduce the generalization gap; limitations are acknowledged.
Reproducibility is generally good: detailed hyperparameters, model choices, prompts, computational cost accounting, and data selection are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is moderate: the work combines existing ingredients—diffusion-based augmentation, teacher-student disagreement, null-text inversion, prompt-to-prompt editing, inter-class mixing—and the core idea is close to ActGen, adapted to knowledge distillation.

The theoretical analysis relies on strong assumptions (accurate well-calibrated teacher, bounded KL, sufficient confidence gap, etc.) that are not directly verified for ConfiG's generated distribution; it motivates but does not prove the method's success.

Evaluation is limited to image classification with relatively modest, often artificially constructed group-shift datasets; there is no full ImageNet-scale, detection, or segmentation evaluation, and the method's usefulness for broader vision tasks remains unclear.

The CelebA-HQ protocol swaps the original train/test splits (training on the original test set and evaluating on the original train set), which is non-standard and may complicate comparability with prior work.
The method relies on access to a robust teacher and an auxiliary student; performance degrades with weaker teachers, and in many real scenarios such a reliable teacher may not be available.

Baseline comparison focuses on diffusion-based augmentation methods; other robust KD or group-robustness approaches without group labels are not extensively compared, and the computational overhead of diffusion generation remains substantial.
Failure cases and hyperparameter sensitivity are acknowledged, but practical guidance for mitigating them and broader societal/bias implications are not deeply discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: knowledge distillation under covariate shift and spurious correlations, with a clear motivating example in Fig. 1.
It proposes ConfG, which combines diffusion-based data augmentation with teacher-student confidence disagreement and inter-class mixing, leveraging foundation models in a data-centric pipeline.

The empirical study is broad: four datasets, group-wise metrics (SMA/GMA/WGA), comparisons to six diffusion-based augmentation baselines, ImageNet-100 spurious evaluation, multiple ablations, computational-cost estimates, and failure-case analysis.
The appendix provides theoretical motivation and detailed reproducibility information (hyperparameters, dataset construction, baseline configurations).
Qualitative examples and teacher-student disagreement analyses support the intuition that test samples from groups absent in training drive distillation failures.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is incremental: ConfG combines existing components (Diff-Mix-style inter-class mixing, DiG-IN/prompt-to-prompt latent optimization, adversarial/hard-example generation) with a straightforward confidence-disagreement loss; the core idea of generating teacher-student-disagreement samples is closely related to active learning and prior augmentation work.

Theoretical Proposition 1 relies on strong, essentially unverifiable assumptions: teacher accurate in KL on all supports (including Q), augmentations more challenging for the student than the teacher, and constants (Theta, Delta_p, alpha) that the authors admit are infeasible to estimate in practice. No empirical validation of these assumptions is provided, so the theory does not convincingly justify the method.

Empirical gains are modest and inconsistent: on BAR, ConfG does not outperform Diff-Mix in SMA (58.66 vs 59.28), and on ImageNet-100 results are single-run without error bars, making many improvements not clearly significant; standard deviations are large across group-shift datasets.

The experimental setup does not really test unknown covariate shift: groups/spurious attributes are manually controlled and removed from training, and the method still assumes access to a robust pretrained teacher; this limits the claim to curated group-shift benchmarks rather than arbitrary real-world shifts.

The method is computationally expensive (Stable Diffusion, iterative latent optimization, auxiliary student training, teacher inference), which conflicts with the resource-constrained motivation for knowledge distillation; FLOP-matched baseline multipliers are approximate and may not account for all overheads.

The confidence-guided objective may amplify teacher overconfidence and spurious correlations rather than preserve causal, label-relevant features; label preservation is not guaranteed, and the paper notes failure cases but does not systematically solve them.

Baseline tuning and comparison may be unfair: most baselines use default hyperparameters, while ConfG benefits from customized inter-class mixing, prompt engineering, and rejection/early-stopping mechanisms; no code is mentioned for reproducibility.
